result:
The proposed answer of 4 cannot be right, because a simple rotation argument shows that any such graph has at least 5 longest paths. The proposed solution also cites a "Walther graph on 18 vertices" with exactly 4 longest paths, and I can't confirm that example.

**Setup.** Let P = v1 v2 … vm be a longest path in a connected graph with minimum degree 3. Paths are counted up to reversal. Since P is longest, every neighbor of v1 and every neighbor of vm lies on P.

**Rotating at v1.** The vertex v1 has at least two neighbors vi and vj on P other than v2, with 2 < i < j. Each one gives a new longest path:
- v_{i-1} … v1 vi … vm, which has ends v_{i-1} and vm.
- v_{j-1} … v1 vj … vm, which has ends v_{j-1} and vm.

**Rotating at vm.** Likewise, vm has at least two neighbors on P other than v_{m-1}. Each gives a longest path with ends v1 and some other vertex v_{k+1}.

**Distinctness.** The five paths have the following end pairs:
- P: {v1, vm}
- Two from v1: each has end vm and an end different from v1.
- Two from vm: each has end v1 and an end different from vm.

Paths from different groups have different end pairs, so they are distinct. Within each group the two paths have different second ends, so they are distinct too.

So there are at least 5 longest paths, and a(3,n) ≥ 5. Hence a(3,n) = 4 is impossible.

VERDICT: REJECT
